concepts.def: A production strategy where materials and components arrive only as they are needed, minimising the stock held and the cost of storage.
Holding buffer stocks of materials and finished goods to protect against demand surges or supply delays, at the cost of extra storage.
An approach that aims to eliminate every form of waste, in time, materials, energy and effort, while still adding value for the customer.
Using computers to control the whole production process, linking design data, manufacturing equipment, materials handling and quality systems together.
Inspecting and testing samples of output against set standards in order to detect and reject defective products after they are made.
Building quality into every stage of the whole production system so that defects are prevented from occurring rather than detected afterwards.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Commercial Production — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Commercial Production brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Commercial Production.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which best describes just in time (JIT) production?
options: Stock arrives just before it is needed, reducing storage costs
Large buffer stocks are held in warehouses
Products are only made one at a time
Quality checks are removed to save time

mcqs.q: The main aim of lean production is to:
options: Maximise the size of the workforce
Eliminate waste while maintaining value for the customer
Increase the amount of stock held
Slow production down to improve quality

mcqs.q: What is the key difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: They are identical processes
QC happens before production, QA afterwards
QC inspects outputs for defects; QA builds quality into the whole process to prevent defects
QA only applies to one-off production
Designers email drawings to the factory
Robots replace every human worker
Only the accounts department uses computers
Computers link and control design, production, handling and quality as one system

mcqs.q: What is the difference between just in time and just in case production?
options: Yes - lean refers to making products lighter in weight.
JIT orders materials to arrive only when needed, cutting storage costs; JIC deliberately holds buffer stock to cope with surprises in supply or demand.
JIT means products are made one at a time by hand.
JIT and JIC are the same system described from two viewpoints.

mcqs.q: Does lean production simply mean employing fewer workers?
options: Yes - lean refers to making products lighter in weight.
No - lean production means systematically eliminating all waste, including overproduction, waiting, defects and excess transport, while preserving customer value.
JIT means products are made one at a time by hand.
Yes - lean means running the factory with the minimum number of staff.

mcqs.q: If a factory has quality control inspectors, does it automatically have quality assurance?
options: No - QC inspection only catches defects after they occur; QA is a wider system that designs processes so defects are prevented in the first place.
Yes - quality control and quality assurance are the same thing.
Yes - lean refers to making products lighter in weight.
Yes - QA is just the modern name for QC.
